text: Every Claude Code session that needs you, in one queue in your terminal. Diffs to review, edits to allow, permission prompts and questions, one card at a time. Linux · tmux · Rust · MIT I run several Claude Code sessions in tmux and kept losing track of which one was waiting on me. aq watches all of them and puts whatever needs me (a diff to review, an edit to allow, a permission prompt, a question) in one queue, shown one card at a time. A card that comes in while I'm on another waits its turn; it never takes the screen. If I answer the card on screen in its own window instead, it stays, marked "answered elsewhere", until I press a key. Tip Quickest install: paste this into Claude Code and let it do the setup. Set up aq (https://github.com/nodo-labs-uk/attention-queue) for me. 1. Install it: download aq-x86_64-linux.tar.gz from the latest release (https://github.com/nodo-labs-uk/attention-queue/releases/latest), or clone the repo and run `cargo install --path .`. Make sure `aq` is on my PATH and `aq --help` runs. 2. Add the three hooks from contrib/settings-hooks.json to ~/.claude/settings.json. Back the file up first. Merge them into the existing PreToolUse, PostToolUse and PermissionRequest arrays, keeping every hook already there, and skip any that are already present. Show me the diff before saving. 3. Check that tmux is installed, and tell me which running Claude sessions need a restart to pick up the hooks. Don't change anything else. Contents: Design principles · Modes · Sessions · Keys · Compared with other tools · Install · Files · Development · Licence Each project has a mode, and M switches it. Review (the default): when a session finishes, its diff becomes a card. You can comment on a line or a range, s sends all the comments, a approves, and d marks a file as done so it's out of the way. Markdown files (plans, specs, READMEs) show as read, with headings, bold, code and bullets styled and their marks hidden; m shows them as written. e opens the file at the cursor's line in your editor, for a change you'd rather make yourself. Step : every edit waits for approval before it's applied. y lets it through, n sends it back with a reason. Quiz : when a session finishes, aq picks the parts of the diff that matter and asks you to explain what they do, or why they were done that way, in your own words. A judge marks the answer. If it isn't right, or you say you don't know, you get a question that leads towards what you missed and another try, twice at most, before the answer is shown ( e shows it sooner). A gap the judge finds in the code itself can be sent back as a fix. Vibe : nothing is checked; the agent just codes. Questions , in every mode: when a session ends its turn by asking you something (to approve a draft, to choose between two ways), its message becomes a card. a approves when the question asks for a go-ahead, Enter replies in your own words, and x puts the card away. When Claude asks with its own menu of options, the card lists them and a number key picks one; the answer goes back through the hook, so nothing is typed into the session. A turn that has both a diff and a question shows the question on the review card, and sending from there answers it. When nothing is waiting, there is a tab per session with the selected one's screen live underneath. Each tab shows the session's permission mode as its footer does, such as ⏵⏵ auto or ⏸ plan . Enter messages it (sent once it's idle), W asks where it's up to without interrupting it, p asks it to open a PR, m switches its model, P its permission mode (auto, manual, accept edits or plan), and Esc Esc stops it. N starts a new Claude session in the same project, in a tmux window of its own, with what you type as its first prompt. Tab in that box gives the session a git worktree of its own (Claude's --worktree ), so two sessions don't edit the same files. Ctrl-O picks another folder: type a path with the matching folders listed underneath ( Tab completes, the arrows choose), and a folder that isn't there yet is made when the session starts. ! opens a shell in a tmux popup, in the project's folder, for things Claude can't run itself: sudo, logins, or commands its permissions block. The last ! command Claude suggested is copied and, in zsh, already typed in, so Enter runs it. The popup closes when the shell exits. The first time aq starts, a tour has you try the workflow on made-up cards, telling you which key to press, one at a time. First a review (move, comment, mark done, send, approve), then M into step mode (allow one edit, refuse the next with a reason), then quiz mode (answer a question and send the gap the judge found back as a fix). Last come three made-up sessions: pick one, message it, ask where it's up to, start a new one and move its project through the modes. Nothing in the tour reaches a real session. F2 runs the tour again, and F1 lists every key. The ones worth knowing from day one: Moving around works as in vim: j k , Ctrl-d Ctrl-u , gg G , ]c [c for changes and H L for files. aq can start a session ( N ), and in a worktree of its own if you ask, but it leaves branches and merging to you and Claude: start Claude however you like and aq picks it up. If you'd rather have one app that manages every session's branch for you, one of the others is a better fit. The prompt at the top of this page does all of this for you. By hand: aq runs on Linux, inside tmux. Either take the binary from the latest release : curl -fsSL https://github.com/nodo-labs-uk/attention-queue/releases/latest/download/aq-x86_64-linux.tar.gz | tar xz install aq-x86_64-linux/aq ~ /.local/bin/ or build it from source with cargo install --path . . Then add the hooks from contrib/settings-hooks.json to ~/.claude/settings.json . Merge them into your existing PreToolUse , PostToolUse and PermissionRequest arrays rather than replacing them, or your other hooks will stop running. docs/hooks.md has the details. Run aq in a tmux window. cargo test runs everything, including end-to-end tests against a private tmux server. demo/record.py re-records the videos with fake sessions and a stand-in claude , so it needs no login and costs nothing. Pushing a v* tag builds a release. MIT : use it, change it and share it, for anything. aq was built with Claude Code . Issues, PRs and other contributions are welcome. You could also point your own agent at this repo and have it build you a version from scratch, but this one saves you the tokens.
